theme.q: A university lets an algorithm decide which applicants are invited for a scholarship interview. It was trained on ten years of past committee decisions and now invites far fewer applicants from vocational schools, although their grades are similar. In the language of AI harms, this is
o: allocational harm
representational harm
myside bias
stochasticity of the output
theme.spot: Who gets an opportunity, not how a group is described.
theme.why: Allocational harm: an AI system hands out resources or opportunities (here: interviews) unequally across groups, because the data contain historically biased decisions. Representational harm would be about how a group is portrayed, for example described as less capable or left out of the picture.
theme.src: [PAST-2][IDQ][CORE] Demszky et al. 2023, Concern 2 (bias); pty_t8 8.5.2

theme.q:
Judge these statements about bias in LLMs (Demszky et al., 2023).
I. Representational harm can arise from sampling bias, for example when the data of privileged groups are over-represented in the training text.
II. Allocational harm means that an LLM describes a social group in a demeaning way.
o: Only statement I is true
Only statement II is true
Both statements are true
Neither statement is true
theme.spot: Portrayal versus distribution.
theme.why: Statement I is true: Demszky et al. name sampling bias (over-represented privileged groups) and data-processing bias as causes of representational harm. Statement II is false: a demeaning description is representational harm. Allocational harm is about the unequal distribution of resources (such as loans) or opportunities (such as therapy).
theme.src: [PAST-2][IDQ A.6][CORE] Demszky et al. 2023, Concern 2; pty_t8 8.5.2

theme.q: Annotators who all belong to the majority culture label chat messages for a training set. They often mark messages written in a minority dialect as 'aggressive', although the writers meant them as friendly banter. A model trained on these labels later rates that dialect as hostile. Where did the bias enter?
o: Data-processing bias in the annotations
Sampling bias in which texts were selected for training
Stochasticity of the model output
Prompt-tuning with too few examples
theme.spot: The texts were there; the labels were wrong.
theme.why: Demszky et al. give exactly this example of data-processing bias: annotators from majority groups misunderstand minority groups, and the model learns their mistakes. Sampling bias would mean the minority texts were missing or under-represented, which is not the problem here. The outcome is representational harm.
theme.src: [IDQ A.6][CORE] Demszky et al. 2023, Concern 2; pty_t8 8.5.2

theme.q: According to Demszky et al. (2023), what makes LLMs more powerful for psychology than earlier text-analysis methods such as LIWC?
o: They approximate word meaning in context and learn from an unprecedented amount and variety of text
They count word categories much faster and rely on dictionaries that psychologists have checked by hand
They check whether statements are true and are trained mainly on peer-reviewed scientific articles
They give every word one stable meaning and need only a few hundred sentences of training text
theme.spot: Two reasons: better modelling and more data.
theme.why: Demszky et al. give two reasons. LLMs go beyond bag-of-words methods by approximating meaning in context, and they are trained on hundreds of billions of utterances from web pages, books, social media and forums. They do not check truth: they predict plausible language, which is why they can give fluent but wrong advice.
theme.src: [PAST-2][CORE] Demszky et al. 2023, Introduction; pty_t8 8.1

theme.q: A classmate says: 'Language AI got so good in the last decade simply because computers became faster.' Which reply fits the course best?
o: Speed helped, but it also took far more training data and better models, such as transformers that read words in context
Speed played no real role; the progress came from programmers who wrote ever more detailed grammar rules for every language by hand
Speed played no real role; the progress came from building psychological theories of truth into the models
Speed helped, but the decisive change was that models now look up each word's one fixed meaning in a dictionary
theme.spot: One ingredient is never the whole story.
theme.why: The jump came from a combination: enormous amounts of training data, huge computing resources to fit models with millions of parameters (fitting ChatGPT is estimated to have cost 3 billion dollars) and better algorithms, such as the transformer that approximates meaning in context. Hand-written rules and fixed dictionary meanings describe the older approaches, and LLMs contain no theory of truth.
theme.src: [PAST-2][CORE] Demszky et al. 2023, Introduction, training, equitable access; pty_t8 8.1, 8.2, 8.6

theme.q: A small neural network must learn to sort photos into 'animate' and 'inanimate'. For a training photo of a dog it outputs 'inanimate'. What happens next during training?
o: The error relative to the correct label is sent back to adjust the connection weights
A new hidden node for 'dog' is added to the network so that this specific example can be stored
The photo is removed from the training set because it confuses the output layer
The network is asked to explain in words why it judged the photo inanimate
theme.spot: Predict, compare, send the error back, repeat.
theme.why: This is back-propagation: the difference between the output and the correct label (the prediction error) is sent back through the network to adjust the weights, and this repeats over many photos. The knowledge lies in the pattern of weights, not in a separate node per concept. LLM pre-training works the same way, with hidden words as the labels.
theme.src: [IDQ A.2][CORE] Demszky et al. 2023, pre-training; pty_t8 8.2, 8.15.2

theme.q: How do bag-of-words methods and LLMs relate to the theories of concepts from Theme 4?
o: Bag-of-words is like the prototype view (one fixed meaning per word); an LLM is like the exemplar view (many uses in context)
Bag-of-words is like the exemplar view (each text stored separately); an LLM is like the prototype view (one average meaning per word)
Both are like the classical view, because they define each word by necessary and sufficient features
Bag-of-words is like the theory view, and an LLM is like the classical view based on definitions
theme.spot: One summary versus many concrete examples in context.
theme.why: A bag-of-words method gives every word one static meaning, like a single summary prototype. An LLM is trained on hundreds of billions of concrete utterances and lets context decide the meaning, like retrieving exemplars. Note the nuance: an LLM also outputs a kind of average of what the internet says, so it has a prototype element too.
theme.src: [IDQ A.3][CORE] pty_t8 8.15.3; Theme 4 link

theme.q: A word-counting program scores the review 'The plot was sick and the ending killed me, I loved it' as strongly negative, because 'sick' and 'killed' are in its negative-emotion dictionary. Which weakness does this show?
o: Each word gets one static meaning, whatever its context
The output varies randomly from one run to the next
The program copies the biases of the human annotators who built it
The program cannot explain how it reached its score
theme.spot: Same word, different company, same score.
theme.why: Bag-of-words programs such as LIWC count dictionary words and assume each word has a static meaning, so slang, sarcasm and metaphor are lost. LLMs approximate meaning in context. Random variation is a property of LLMs (stochasticity), and word counts are actually very transparent, so the black-box problem does not apply.
theme.src: [IDQ A.1][CORE] Demszky et al. 2023, Introduction; pty_t8 8.1, 8.15.1

theme.q: Two labs want a model that recognises 'hopelessness' in diary entries. Lab A pastes five labelled entries into the prompt of a commercial LLM. Lab B trains a pre-trained model further on 500 labelled entries, updating its parameters. Which statement is correct?
o: Lab B is better placed to capture subtle features and correct inherited bias, because its parameters change
Lab A is better placed to correct inherited bias, because a good prompt overrides what the model learned in pre-training
Both approaches change the model's parameters, so the two labs differ only in how fast they work
Lab A is using fine-tuning and Lab B is using prompt-tuning, so Lab A needs more labelled data
theme.spot: Do the parameters change or not?
theme.why: Lab A uses prompt-tuning (in-context learning): a few examples, fast, but the parameters stay unchanged, so it captures subtle constructs less well and is less able to overcome bias. Lab B uses fine-tuning, which updates the parameters. Fine-tuning is costly and can still keep or even amplify bias, depending on who does it.
theme.src: [IDQ A.7][CORE] Demszky et al. 2023, fine-tuning and prompt-tuning; pty_t8 8.4

theme.q: Asked to coach a nervous pupil about her university application, an LLM advised her to 'reduce stress' and 'take breaks', as if stress always hurts performance. Which finding from the lecture on cognition and emotion speaks against this view?
o: Performance is an inverted-U function of arousal, so a moderate level of stress can help
Positive affect combined with low motivational intensity broadens the scope of visual attention
Valence and arousal are independent dimensions on which emotions can be placed
Emotional words slow down colour naming in the emotional Stroop task
theme.spot: Is stress always bad for performance?
theme.why: The Yerkes-Dodson law says performance peaks at a moderate level of arousal, so stress can be enhancing, which is also what Demszky et al. say stress research shows. The LLM gave the common cultural advice (a stress-is-debilitating mindset) because it predicts plausible, not correct, language. The other options are true lecture findings but say nothing about whether stress helps.
theme.src: [IDQ A.4][CORE] Demszky et al. 2023, study-advice example; pty_t8 8.3, 8.15.4; Lecture 3

theme.q: Trained coders, none of whom belong to the group concerned, rate social-media posts by members of a religious minority about their workplace as 'calm and neutral'. The writers themselves say the posts express hurt. Which problem of expert evaluation does this show?
o: The intersubjectivity problem, made worse across group lines
The black-box problem of LLM output
Stochasticity in the coders' ratings
The ambiguity of a null result, a known weakness of impact evaluation
theme.spot: Can an outsider know what the writer meant?
theme.why: Expert evaluation suffers from the intersubjectivity problem: coders guess how someone construes a situation, and they can guess wrong. Demszky et al. note this gets worse in cross-group judgements, especially across power differences. An ambiguous null result is the weakness of impact evaluation, not of expert evaluation.
theme.src: [CORE] Demszky et al. 2023, Concern 1 (evaluation); pty_t8 8.5.1

theme.q:
The table shows results for participants with 30 minutes in Zhi et al. (2026). A lower myside bias score means less one-sided reasoning. Continuous and Late access had a significantly lower myside bias score than No LLM access.
AccessMyside biasNumber of arguments
Early3.794.56
Continuous3.344.42
Late3.425.25
No LLM4.415.12
Which conclusion fits best?
o: Only Late access made essays less one-sided while keeping as many arguments as working alone
Continuous access gave the most balanced essays and also produced the most arguments
Early access made the essays less one-sided than any of the other access conditions
Working without an LLM gave the least one-sided essays, because those participants wrote the most arguments
theme.spot: Look at both columns at once.
theme.why: Late access lowered myside bias (3.42 vs 4.41) while the number of arguments stayed as high as working alone (5.25 vs 5.12): people used the chatbot at the end to add counter-arguments they had overlooked. Continuous access was also less one-sided, but with the fewest arguments. Working alone gave many arguments but the highest (worst) myside bias.
theme.src: [IDQ B.4][CORE] Zhi et al. 2026, Table 4; pty_t8 8.7.2, 8.16.4

theme.q: Suppose access timing and time availability had each influenced essay scores in Zhi et al. (2026), but without any interaction. With access timing on the x-axis and one line per time limit, what would the figure look like?
o: Two roughly parallel lines: the 30-minute line higher everywhere and the same ranking of access conditions at both time limits
Two lines that cross: Early access best at 10 minutes, but Late and No access best at 30 minutes
Two lines lying on top of each other, with Early access scoring highest at both time limits
One line rising and the other falling, so that the effects of the two time limits cancel each other out when averaged over conditions
theme.spot: No interaction means parallel lines.
theme.why: Without an interaction, the effect of access timing is the same at both time limits, so the lines run parallel; a main effect of time only shifts one line up. The real data showed crossing lines: Early was best at 10 minutes (3.80) but scored below No access at 30 minutes (4.51 vs 5.76). That temporal reversal is the interaction.
theme.src: [IDQ B.1, B.2][CORE] Zhi et al. 2026, Fig. 4a (illustrative counterfactual); pty_t8 8.7.2, 8.16.1

theme.q: After the main task, Zhi et al. (2026) asked participants to rate their own critical thinking on a self-assessment scale. What did these self-ratings show?
o: Only slight differences, linked to time availability but not to LLM access timing
Large differences that closely mirrored the temporal reversal found in the essay scores
Higher ratings after Early access, in line with this group's better recall
Lower ratings without LLM access, because that group felt the most rushed
theme.spot: Did people notice the effect of the chatbot on their own thinking?
theme.why: Self-ratings barely differed and only time availability made any difference, while essay scores and recall differed substantially. The authors conclude that self-reports miss how LLMs affect thinking, because people have limited awareness of their own time use and subtle cognitive changes, so performance assessment is needed. Early access actually went with worse recall.
theme.src: [IDQ B.5][CORE] Zhi et al. 2026, self-reported assessment; pty_t8 8.7.3

theme.q: A university board fears that students will let chatbots write their take-home essays and is weighing its options. Which policy fits the findings of Zhi et al. (2026) best?
o: Keep the essays and the generous time, but require an outline written without a chatbot before chatbot use is allowed
Replace the essays with 10-minute timed tasks in which a chatbot is available right from the start
Keep the essays and allow the chatbot throughout the whole task, since the students' self-ratings showed no harm from it
Ban chatbots altogether, because chatbot access lowered essay scores in every condition of the study
theme.spot: Plenty of time: own work first, chatbot later.
theme.why: With enough time, people who worked alone first scored best (Late 5.77, No access 5.76) and those with access from the start scored lower (Early 4.51) and remembered the sources worse. So keep the essay but sequence it: own thinking first, chatbot later. A ban ignores that under time pressure early access helped (3.80 vs 2.75), and self-ratings are not a valid guide.
theme.src: [IDQ B.5][CORE] Zhi et al. 2026, practical implications; pty_t8 8.8, 8.16.5

theme.q:
Judge these statements about the essay scores in Zhi et al. (2026).
I. In every access-timing condition, participants with 30 minutes had a higher mean essay score than participants with 10 minutes.
II. Which access timing worked best depended on how much time participants had.
o: Only statement I is true
Only statement II is true
Both statements are true
Neither statement is true
theme.spot: Check each row, then ask whether the ranking flips.
theme.why: Statement I is true: every condition scored higher with 30 minutes (Early 3.80 to 4.51, Continuous 3.49 to 4.71, Late 1.86 to 5.77, No access 2.75 to 5.76), a main effect of time. Statement II is true too: Early was best under time pressure, Late and No access with enough time. A ranking that flips across levels of the other factor is an interaction.
theme.src: [IDQ B.1][CORE] Zhi et al. 2026, Tables 3 and 4; pty_t8 8.7.2

theme.q: A researcher repeats Huang's (2025) design with a poetry-writing task. The figure shows mean creativity ratings (illustrative data). Do these results support the Goldilocks effect?

chart.title: Creativity by level of AI collaboration (illustrative)

o: No, because high collaboration scores highest, so the pattern is linear rather than an inverted U
Yes, because moderate collaboration scores higher than low collaboration
Yes, because all three levels of AI collaboration produce fairly creative poems
No, because an inverted U would require low collaboration to score highest of the three conditions
theme.spot: Where is the peak?
theme.why: The Goldilocks effect is an inverted U: moderate collaboration must beat both low and high. Here creativity keeps rising up to high collaboration, which is the linear 'more AI, better' pattern Huang argued against. Beating low collaboration alone is not enough.
theme.src: [IDQ C.3][CORE] Huang 2025 hypothesis; pty_t8 8.9 (illustrative chart)

theme.q: Theme 7 treats restructuring the problem as a key route to insight. How do Huang's (2025) findings relate to this?
o: AI collaboration did not change problem restructuring; it affected creativity through the diversity of ideas
Moderate AI collaboration helped people restructure the problem, and that restructuring explained the creativity gain
High AI collaboration blocked problem restructuring, and that is why creativity dropped at high collaboration
Low AI collaboration produced the most restructuring, because people stayed with their own perspective
theme.spot: Which mediator was significant?
theme.why: In Studies 1 and 2, problem restructuring did not differ between conditions; knowledge diversity did, and it mediated the inverted U. So AI collaboration did not change how people reframe a problem ('thinking outside the box', the preparation-focused process) but how many different ideas they produced (the production-focused process).
theme.src: [IDQ C.4][CORE] Huang 2025, Studies 1-2 and Discussion; pty_t8 8.9.2, 8.12

theme.q: A call centre wants staff to draft standard, easily recognisable replies to frequent customer questions; originality is not wanted. Based on the mechanism behind Huang's (2025) Goldilocks effect, how much AI use makes sense?
o: More AI use is defensible, because the standardised output that harms creativity is what this task needs
Moderate use is still best, since four to six prompts was shown to be the optimum for any kind of task or goal
As little AI use as possible, because the AI's ideas would anchor the staff to expected answers
No AI use at all, because AI lowers the knowledge diversity of the replies in every task
theme.spot: What harms creativity may help a different goal.
theme.why: Heavy AI use hurts creativity because AI gives standardised responses and anchors people to expected ideas. When a common, recognisable answer is the goal, that downside becomes the point, so more AI use is defensible (still checking the output). The four-to-six rule came from one 15-minute task and was never shown to hold for every task.
theme.src: [IDQ C.4] Huang 2025 mechanism; pty_t8 8.17.4
theme.hy: 20. Applying Huang to a new task

theme.q: In Huang's first two studies, participants were told to use ChatGPT once, four to six times, or at least nine times. A critic says participants may have guessed what the researcher expected and behaved accordingly. What is this concern called?
o: Demand effects
Common-method bias
Myside bias
Anchoring
theme.spot: Participants reacting to the study itself.
theme.why: Demand effects (expectancy bias) arise when participants act on what they think the study is about. Huang ran Study 3, a field study without manipulation, partly to rule them out. Common-method bias is a different problem (both measures from the same source at the same time), which Study 3 reduced by having supervisors rate creativity a week later.
theme.src: [IDQ C.2][CORE] Huang 2025, Study 3; pty_t8 8.11, 8.17.2

theme.q: In Huang (2025), human-rated and AI-rated creativity correlated positively, at about r = .23. What does this mean?
o: The measures are related, but only modestly: a high score on one does not reliably mean a high score on the other
The measures are practically interchangeable, so AI ratings could replace the human raters
The measures are unrelated, because any correlation below .50 counts as no relation
The AI rated the proposals as 23 percent more creative on average than the human raters did, so AI ratings are inflated
theme.spot: r is about how closely scores go together.
theme.why: r = .23 is a weak positive correlation: a wide cloud of points with a slight upward trend. Huang calls the correlations between creativity measures significant but modest, so different raters may weigh different aspects (experts profit, the crowd writing quality, AI perhaps novelty). A correlation says nothing about mean differences.
theme.src: [IDQ C.1][CORE] Huang 2025, limitations; pty_t8 8.12.2, 8.17.1

theme.q: The Texas Mindset Initiative records 1,000 high-school teachers talking with students, annotates the talk for constructs such as growth mindset and autonomy support, and links it to student performance over time. Which investment proposed by Demszky et al. (2023) does this illustrate?
o: A keystone dataset
A psychologically defined benchmark
Equitable access to LLMs
Prompt-tuning with expert examples
theme.spot: Large, expert-annotated, linked to outcomes.
theme.why: A keystone dataset is a large natural-language database that meets high standards for expert and impact evaluation and is linked to important outcomes. Benchmarks are standard tasks on which models are compared, and equitable access is about affordable models and shared infrastructure.
theme.src: [CORE] Demszky et al. 2023, three investments; pty_t8 8.6

theme.q: With 30 minutes for the task, which judgement did participants with Continuous LLM access make significantly worse than participants without LLM access in Zhi et al. (2026)?
o: Judging how reliable each source document was
Judging the stance each document took
Judging the relevance of each document to the decision
Judging factual and counterfactual statements
theme.spot: Continuous help, less own checking.
theme.why: Under sufficient time, Continuous access gave worse judgements of source reliability (34.0%) than No LLM access (44.3%), possibly because constant chatbot help led to less of their own critical checking of credibility. Comprehension and the other evaluation measures depended mainly on time, with little effect of access timing.
theme.src: [CORE] Zhi et al. 2026, Section 4.4, Table 4; pty_t8 8.7.2

theme.q: The figure shows recall of the main ideas of the documents in Zhi et al. (2026). Which statement is NOT supported?

chart.title: Recall score by LLM access timing

o: Under 10 minutes, Continuous access led to significantly worse recall than No LLM access
With 30 minutes, Continuous access led to significantly worse recall than No LLM access
Extra time raised recall more for those who started on their own than for those with access from the start
At 30 minutes, none of the chatbot conditions recalled the documents better than No LLM access
theme.spot: Check which time limit the significant difference belongs to.
theme.why: Under 10 minutes, recall did not differ significantly between conditions (1.85 to 2.11). The significant drop is at 30 minutes: Continuous 2.03 vs No access 2.99 (Early 2.23 only marginal). Late and No access gained most from extra time. Early AI help seems to hinder internalisation of the sources.
theme.src: [IDQ B.3][CORE] Zhi et al. 2026, Fig. 4b, Tables 3 and 4; pty_t8 8.7.2, 8.16.3

theme.q:
A researcher sends an LLM the same request for career advice 50 times per version, changing only the name: 'Emma' or 'Daniel'. The table (hypothetical data) shows how often a leadership role was suggested.
Name in promptLeadership role suggested
Emma18%
Daniel41%
Which conclusion fits this method best?
o: The output differs with the gender cue, but biases tied to traits she did not vary, or to combinations of traits, stay hidden
The LLM is unbiased, because a stochastic model always gives different answers to the same prompt
The difference only counts as bias if the LLM itself explains that it took the names into account
The design cannot show bias, because the two prompts should have differed in more than the name alone to be a fair test
theme.spot: Change one cue, compare outputs: what can and cannot it show?
theme.why: This is the audit method: keep the prompt identical, vary only the name or pronoun, generate many responses (LLMs are stochastic) and compare. A systematic gap points to bias. Its limit: you only see biases you vary explicitly, so unknown biases and intersectionality stay hidden. Asking the LLM to explain itself is circular.
theme.src: [IDQ A.8][CORE] Demszky et al. 2023, Concern 2; pty_t8 8.5.2, 8.15.8 (hypothetical table)

m1.q: An online platform's advertising algorithm, trained on past click data, shows adverts for well-paid engineering jobs mostly to men. Which kind of AI harm is this, and why?
o: Allocational, because an opportunity is distributed unequally between groups
Representational, because women are portrayed in a demeaning way
Representational, because the training data over-represent men
Allocational, because the algorithm's output varies from one run to the next
m1.why: Job opportunities reach one group more than another, so this is allocational harm, rooted in historically biased patterns in the data. Representational harm is about how a group is depicted. Variation between runs is stochasticity, not a harm.

m1.q: The figure shows mean essay scores in Zhi et al. (2026) for participants who had only 10 minutes. Early and Continuous access scored significantly higher than Late access. Which conclusion is correct?
o: Under time pressure, help from the start paid off, while help only at the end did not
Under time pressure, any form of chatbot access raised scores above working alone
Under time pressure, Late access gave the best essays because participants first worked alone
Under time pressure, scores did not depend on when the chatbot was available
m1.spot: Find the highest and the lowest bar.
m1.why: With 10 minutes, Early (3.80) and Continuous (3.49) were highest and Late was lowest (1.86), even below No access (2.75): help that comes in the last third is too late to use. So not every form of access helped. With 30 minutes this ranking reverses, the temporal reversal.
m1.src: [IDQ B.2][CORE] Zhi et al. 2026, Table 3, Fig. 4a; pty_t8 8.7.2

m1.q: A design agency lets three teams brainstorm a campaign with a chatbot. Team A may prompt it once, Team B a handful of times, Team C as often as it likes and does so constantly. According to Huang (2025), which creativity ranking is most likely?
o: B above both A and C, with A and C about equal
C above B, and B above A, since more prompts give more ideas
A above B, and B above C
A and C equal, and both above B
m1.spot: Not too little, not too much.
m1.why: Huang found an inverted U: moderate collaboration (4.02 in Study 1) beat low (3.49) and high (3.39), and low and high did not differ. Too little AI limits the range of perspectives; too much brings standardised ideas and anchoring.

m2.q: Which of these is NOT a reason why language AI became so powerful in recent years?
o: Models were given rules for checking whether statements are true
Models were trained on hundreds of billions of utterances from many sources
Transformer models approximate the meaning of words in their context
Huge computing budgets made it possible to fit models with millions of parameters
m2.spot: Which one describes something LLMs do not do?
m2.why: Progress came from data (hundreds of billions of utterances), better models (transformers that approximate meaning in context) and enormous resources to fit the parameters. LLMs do not check truth: they predict plausible language, which is why they can sound convincing and still be wrong.
m2.src: [PAST-2][CORE] Demszky et al. 2023, Introduction, training, equitable access; pty_t8 8.1-8.3, 8.6

m2.q: In Zhi et al. (2026), extra time (30 instead of 10 minutes) helped participants with Late or No access much more than participants with Early or Continuous access. Which explanation do the authors give?
o: Early chatbot output anchored their thinking, so they added few arguments of their own and went back to the documents less
Early-access participants spent the extra time checking the chatbot's facts, which slowed down their writing
Late-access participants copied larger parts of the chatbot's answers into their essays than the others
Early-access participants felt more time pressure, because they had to share their limited time between the chatbot and the task
m2.spot: What did early help do to their own thinking?
m2.why: With extra time, Early and Continuous participants barely added unique arguments (+0.28 and +0.07) and consulted the documents less while writing, whereas Late and No access added many (+1.80 and +2.10). They had seen more valid arguments from the chatbot, but stayed anchored to it instead of thinking beyond it.
m2.src: [IDQ B.5][CORE] Zhi et al. 2026, Figs. 7-8; pty_t8 8.7.2

m2.q: Huang (2025) found that moderate AI collaboration raised the knowledge diversity of brainstormed ideas, and that this diversity in turn raised creativity. In this analysis, knowledge diversity is a
o: mediator
moderator
manipulated independent variable
control variable
m2.spot: It explains how X affects Y.
m2.why: A mediator lies between cause and outcome and explains how the effect comes about (collaboration, then diversity, then creativity). A moderator changes the strength of an effect, such as skill level, which Huang names as an untested boundary condition. Knowledge diversity was measured, not manipulated, so the mediation is correlational.

m3.q: A face-recognition system works well for light-skinned faces but often fails for dark-skinned faces, because most training photos showed light-skinned people. Which source of bias and which fix fit the course best?
o: Sampling bias; fine-tune the model on well-annotated photos of under-represented groups
Data-processing bias; set the temperature to 0 so that the model's output becomes stable
Sampling bias; ask the model to explain which kinds of faces it finds difficult
Stochasticity; generate many outputs per photo and average them
m3.spot: Who was missing from the training data?
m3.why: Too few photos of one group is sampling bias, leading to representational harm. Fine-tuning on representative, well-annotated data updates the parameters so the model learns those faces, ideally with people from the target group involved. Asking a model to explain itself is circular, and temperature only controls output variability.
m3.src: [IDQ A.6, A.7][CORE] Demszky et al. 2023; pty_t8 8.15.6, 8.15.7

m3.q: Probing an LLM resembles an experiment in psychology. Which mapping is correct?
o: The manipulated linguistic feature is the independent variable; the model's output is the dependent variable
The model's output is the independent variable; the manipulated linguistic feature is the dependent variable
The model's own explanation of its answer is the dependent variable; the original prompt is the control condition
The temperature setting is the independent variable; the training data are the dependent variable
m3.spot: What do you change, what do you measure?
m3.why: In probing you pick a feature (such as negation), change the input along it ('I care' vs 'I don't care') and compare the output: the feature is the independent variable, the output the dependent variable. Like testing many participants, you generate many responses per prompt. Asking the LLM to explain itself is circular.
m3.src: [IDQ A.5][CORE] Demszky et al. 2023, Concern 3; pty_t8 8.5.3, 8.15.5

m3.q: In Huang's Study 3, supervisor-rated creativity was predicted from creative professionals' self-reported AI collaboration. The linear term was positive and significant; the quadratic term was negative and significant. Which curve does this describe?
o: Creativity rises with AI use up to a moderate level and then declines
Creativity rises steadily with AI use, without any turning point
Creativity falls at moderate AI use and rises again at high AI use
Creativity is unrelated to AI use once the control variables are added
m3.why: A positive linear term with a negative quadratic term gives an inverted U (here not perfectly symmetric) with a turning point around moderate AI use. The pattern held with the control variables and was less consistent without them. Because Study 3 is correlational, it supports the Goldilocks pattern and weakens demand effects, but does not prove causation.
